title: UNH, HUM, CNC Stocks Rally On Medicare Advantage Rate Surprise - Stocktwits
content: Shares of insurers UnitedHealth Group (UNH), Centene (CNC), Humana (HUM), and Elevance Health (ELV) jumped in Monday’s extended trading hours after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the payments to private insurers offering Medicare Advantage plans will increase 2.48% next year. This increase implies $13 billion in additional payments to Medicare insurers for the year, the agency said. “When accounting for estimated risk score trend in MA due to factors such as population changes and coding practices, this amounts to a 4.98% increase,” the agency added. The move came as a surprise since in January, the CMS had proposed a roughly flat increase in payments for private Medicare plans the following year, sending shares of insurers down and wiping out about $100 billion in stock market value. The announcement further comes as a relief to the industry plagued by concerns over rising medical costs. Shares of UNH, CNC, HUM and ELV rallied between 5% and 11% at the time of writing. Shares of Aetna parent CVS Health (CVS) rose by about 6.5% while Molina Healthcare (MOH) stock rose a modest 3%. While UnitedHealth is the largest provider of private Medicare Advantage plans in the U.S., Humana is the second largest. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around UNH stock rose from ‘bullish’ to ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume increased from ‘normal’ to ‘high’ levels. Sentiment around HUM stock, meanwhile, increased from ‘neutral’ to ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past 24 hours, while message volume rose from ‘normal’ to ‘extremely high’ levels. A Stocktwits user expressed hopes for Wall Street analysts weighing in on the impact of the rate on UNH stock on Tuesday. Yet another user noted that analysts were expecting a lower rate. While UNH stock fell 46% over the past 12 months, HUM stock fell 28%. The company is seeking approval for ReNu in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis pain, a degenerative joint disease that is estimated to affect nearly 31.1 million Americans. title: Keeping Local Produce Safe: N.H. Farmers Get Assistance from Extension - University of New Hampshire
content: You know that water is necessary for growing plants, but you might be surprised just how much your local farmer thinks about their water. Water isn’t just used for irrigation, it’s also needed as a vehicle to deliver fertilizer and to wash produce after harvest. And, as the current cyclospora outbreak is highlighting, water can also be a source of disease-causing contamination. Farmers in New Hampshire have the support of UNH Extension, which has programs to help design water usage systems that will both provide for sustainable harvests and reduce risks of water-borne pathogens such as cyclospora. And, according to Wendy Johnecheck, state specialist and associate professor for Extension, consumers should feel confident consuming fresh produce from local farms, as there’s no evidence linking a New Hampshire farm to the current outbreak, which has sickened thousands across the country. That’s a credit, says Johnacheck, to the work that farms across the state have done to stay up-to-date with best practices around water management and use, often with help and guidance from Extension. “We’re the support system,” Johnecheck says. “The farmers are front-and-center.” Extension supports for local farmers range from online resources to on-farm visits to the newest effort, a program that will help farmers to build what Johnacheck calls a “water budget,” a report that details how much water a farm will need in a given year, so that the farmer can plan ahead for where they will get that water. When it comes to best practices for water safety, Johnecheck says that many farmers are already where they ought to be. For example, drip irrigation is often utilized because of its efficiency. It’s also a safe way to irrigate, as for most produce the water doesn’t contact the part of the plant that’s eaten. Consumers can also be assured that farms are required follow certain practices defined by the Food Safety Modernization Act, enforced by the state’s Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food, which require regular, documented inspections and maintenance of agricultural water systems, and testing for E. coli if untreated groundwater is used to wash produce after harvest. Extension provides resources to assist farmers in complying with these rules, and hosts meetings for farmers to get together and learn about how their colleagues are addressing shared problems. “New Hampshire growers are doing an amazing job in investing in all these resources. Some of these hazards and risks are risks are age old, and some of these are evolving anew,” says Johnecheck. “It takes infrastructure. It takes money. It takes investment for them to be doing it. They're continuing to evolve. We're continuing to work with them. Water is one of our key areas that we're working on.” For general information about Ccyclospora in New Hampshire, visit www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/disease-prevention/infectious-disease-control/cyclosporiasis. For information targeted to growers, visit extension.unh.edu/blog/2026/07/production-practices-protect-nh-crops-cyclospora-contamination. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Why Did AAPL, ATAI, UNH Stocks Jump To 52-Week Highs Today? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Apple Inc. (AAPL), AtaiBeckley Inc. (ATAI), and UnitedHealth Group Inc. (UNH) jumped to 52-week highs on Thursday amid company-specific triggers, Wall Street optimism, and strong earnings results. AAPL stock closed up nearly 2% higher on Thursday as Apple Intelligence AI service registration in China, alongside Wall Street optimism over the company’s recent strength, bolstered prices. ATAI stock jumped more than 33% at close after Eli Lilly (LLY) confirmed that it is acquiring the clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company. Meanwhile, UNH stock gained more than 1% after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings blew past Wall Street estimates and it also raised its full-year profit outlook. Shares of the iPhone maker clocked an all-time high of $334.68 on Thursday amid a series of positive catalysts for the company. China's cyberspace regulator on Wednesday approved the registration of Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones in the country, clearing a key regulatory hurdle for the long-awaited launch of Apple's AI features in the country. Under Chinese rules, companies must obtain approval for large language models and generative AI services before releasing them to the public. Apple Intelligence is expected to leverage AI models from Baidu and Alibaba. Meanwhile, HSBC upgraded AAPL stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold,’ with a price target of $366, implying an upside of 10% from the stock’s last close. Apple has drawn increased attention in recent weeks after it announced hikes in prices for several products, including MacBooks, iPads, HomePods and Apple TV devices, fueling speculation that iPhone price increases could follow. Investors are also focused on the company's upcoming leadership change, with John Ternus set to succeed Tim Cook as CEO on Sept. 1. AAPL stock has risen nearly 23% so far in 2026, while retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing. Shares of the psychedelics company surged to a yearly high of $7.22 after pharma giant Eli Lilly (LLY) confirmed its acquisition of AtaiBeckley. Eli Lilly said that it will acquire all outstanding ATAI shares for $6.75 per share in cash, with shareholders eligible for an additional up to $2.50 per share if certain development and regulatory milestones are achieved, bringing the deal's total potential value to $9.25 per share. The cash offer represents a 25.9% premium to ATAI's Wednesday closing price, while the maximum consideration implies a 72.6% premium. The acquisition is expected to close in the third quarter (Q3) of this year. ATAI stock is up more than 84% this year. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was in the ‘extremely bullish’ territory at the time of writing. UNH stock touched a 52-week high of $461.62 in Thursday’s trading session after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings results blew past Wall Street estimates. The company posted revenue of $112.03 billion, up about 0.37% from $111.62 billion in the prior-year quarter. However, it beat Wall Street expectations of $110.9 billion, as per Fiscal.ai estimates. Meanwhile, net income came in at $5.48 billion, or $6.04 per share, compared with $3.41 billion, or $3.74 per share, in the same period a year ago. The health insurer now expects 2026 adjusted earnings of $19.50 to $20 per share, up from its prior outlook of more than $18.25 per share, while maintaining its revenue guidance of more than $439 billion for the year. The company attributed the better-than-expected results and higher full-year profit outlook to improved management of elevated medical costs and greater use of AI to streamline operations. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) suffered their worst one-day drop in more than two years on Thursday after a $1 billion convertible-note raise rattled investors, but options veteran Jon Najarian said that the deal still represents “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” ASTS stock plunged 17% on Thursday to close at $55.01, marking its lowest closing level of the year. Najarian and his brother Pete Najarian broke down the financing and ASTS’ selloff in a Market Rebellion video posted on X. The brothers co-founded Market Rebellion, an options-focused market analysis platform, in 2016. AST SpaceMobile priced $1 billion of 1.625% convertible senior notes due in 2034, with an initial conversion price of $79.57 per share, which was about 20% above Wednesday’s close. Jon Najarian said that the notes give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to convert into ASTS shares at that price. While the 1.625% coupon is relatively low, he said the real appeal lies in the potential equity upside. “If the stock’s 200 bucks, you’re still exercising it at $79.57,” he said, calling the structure “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” The $200 figure was a hypothetical example, not a formal price target. Pete Najarian said that investors were focused on the risk that the notes could eventually convert into shares and dilute existing holders. “They’re concerned about dilution and all the rest of it,” he said, adding that the stock’s negative reaction was “understandable.” Still, he agreed the financing could support a valuable long-term opportunity. “I think this could be something into the future that could be pretty special, quite frankly,” he said. The brothers also stressed that ASTS remains a highly volatile trade. Implied volatility in the options was around 100%, according to Pete Najarian. “The implied volatility of this thing is not a joke,” he said. “Hell yes, this thing is volatile.” AST SpaceMobile said proceeds remaining after capped-call transactions may be used to secure additional access to orbit through “partnerships and/or acquisitions.” The company said the move could further vertically integrate its business and reduce reliance on third-party launch providers, although it currently has no agreement for any transaction. Satellite communications analyst Tim Farrar said that the language pointed to a potential acquisition. Potential names raised included United Launch Alliance, Firefly Aerospace, Relativity Space and Stoke Space. Farrar also said that AST may be trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertically integrated model across launch and satellite infrastructure. “ASTS were outbid for Iridium, so it looks like they are now trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertical integration play,” he said. The Najarians also suggested acquisitions may be part of the plan. “They’ve got some ideas with partnerships, acquisitions, all that kind of thing that people are excited about,” Jon Najarian said. “They just needed the capital,” he added. The financing comes as AST SpaceMobile continues expanding its BlueBird satellite network. BlueBird 10 recently deployed its communications array in low Earth orbit, while BlueBirds 8 and 9 are next. BlueBird 11 has arrived at Cape Canaveral, and BlueBirds 12 and 13 are being transported from Texas to Florida. AST said that the newer satellites are expected to deliver nearly twice the peak speeds of its first-generation spacecraft. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for ASTS slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid ‘high’ message volume. A Stocktwits poll with more than 2,000 votes showed retail traders largely remained bullish despite the selloff, with 49% saying they were "buying the dip," while 21% were waiting for a better entry, 19% planned to hold their positions, and just 11% said they were selling or trimming. A July 21 poll published by the University of New Hampshire reports that Governor Phil Scott’s approval rating has fallen below 50%, his lowest rating since university polling began surveying Vermont in 2022. The poll found that 48% of Vermont residents approve of Scott’s job performance, while 43% disapprove. Eight percent were neutral or unsure. 20 percent of respondents strongly disapproved of Scott, whereas only 15% strongly approved of the governor. The poll surveyed 1,119 Vermont residents online between July 15 and 20. It included 954 likely general election voters, 560 likely Democratic primary voters and 220 likely Republican primary voters. This decline in approval comes as Scott prepares to seek a sixth term as governor and is running unopposed for the Republican nomination. If reelected, he would become the longest-serving governor in Vermont history, beating out Howard Dean who served from August 1991 to January 2003. Scott won reelection in 2024 with 73% of the vote. Among respondents who disapprove of Scott’s job performance, his handling of education was the most common reason cited. Coincidentally, education is also cited as the most common reason for approval of his performance. His handling of healthcare was the second most common issue, followed by respondents who cited poor leadership. Scott’s approval remains strongest among Republicans, with 60% approving of his performance. Forty-five percent of Democrats and 45% of independents also said they approve of the governor. The person who governs all of New Hampshire's public universities could also be the leader of its largest, after a recommendation by the organization overseeing them. The University System of New Hampshire's Board of Trustees held a vote June 25-26 in favor of the recommendation. If state lawmakers approve, it would merge the roles of USNH chancellor and University of New Hampshire president into a single position. The president would also serve as chancellor overseeing Keene State College and Plymouth State University, the two other schools under the USNH umbrella, with both schools' presidents reporting to that office. The change would modify the current law under Chapter 187-A, which sets parameters for state colleges. All three institutions would remain separate. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << Current chancellor Catherine Provencher said she and the presidents of all three schools were tasked in March with coming up with an idea to improve future leadership. UNH enrolls 70% of the system's students, and accounts for 80% of its costs. Provencher said out of all three schools, the university's scale made it the logical home for shared services now housed in the Chancellor's office. Human resources, procurement, and accounting could also have additional staff if the organization sees it as beneficial. The recommendation comes as New Hampshire's public universities face financial pressure and sinking enrollment. The state ranks last in the nation for public higher education funding, according to the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute. The number of students attending class has also gone down, as fewer traditional college-age students choose four-year institutions. Provencher said the consolidation would improve the speed of decision-making and overall efficiency, without sacrificing independence. "It will align business processes and practices for consistency across our entire enterprise," Provencher said. "Then we can build strength across all three institutions." Provencher said USNH consulted with other university systems around the country that already operate under the proposed model, including the University of Houston system and Washington state's system. She emphasized that the change would not amount to folding the smaller schools into UNH. "Those institutions are integral to the economic health of those regions of our state and our state as a whole," she said. George Hansel, a USNH trustee, voted against the recommendation. He said the proposal raises unanswered questions about how one person can balance the needs of a large university with two smaller campuses. "There is an urgent need for change. No one is denying that," Hansel said. "(But) I think there are multiple solutions, or multiple things, that our institutions need to do to innovate and remain relevant." Hansel said his main concern was preserving the autonomy of Keene State and Plymouth State. "I want to make sure as a trustee, that each of our individual institutions has the room to run, the room to innovate, and come up with a path that really just serves the needs of their local communities," he said. He added that he welcomes the legislature's involvement, as it would open up broader conversations about the decision. "We do have to be careful as we move forward and make sure we're really thinking about this holistically and in a way that allows us to utilize the fact that we're a small state with a small system," Hansel said. The New Hampshire Legislature needs to approve the changes before the merger can take effect. If cleared, the positions would combine on July 1, 2027. title: UNH lands $8M grant to study ticks and tickborne diseases - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: This story was originally produced by the New Hampshire Bulletin, an independent local newsroom that allows NHPR and other outlets to republish its reporting. New Hampshire’s ticks are having a moment, prompting the state’s scientists to come together in hopes of better understanding, and combating, the problem. An $8 million grant from the National Science Foundation will support an investigation into how factors like climate, habitat, wildlife, and more affect the parasites and the diseases they spread, according to a release shared by the University of New Hampshire on Wednesday. “Ticks are an issue that touches nearly every community in New Hampshire,” said David Needle, a University of New Hampshire professor and veterinary pathologist leading the four-year project, in the release. Scientists from the University of New Hampshire, Keene State University, and Plymouth State University, and students, state agencies, and private industry will collaborate on the initiative. The announcement comes as ticks, and the various illnesses they carry, pose an increasing risk to the health of humans and wildlife alike. Emergency room visits for tick bites surged this summer, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And while tick-borne illnesses that have been increasingly common for decades, like Lyme disease, remain both prevalent and dangerous, diseases that have emerged more recently are on the rise, too. Warmer winters, driven by climate change, have helped tick populations gain ground, aided by development and shifts in wildlife populations, according to the release. Scientists participating in the study will come from various fields to participate in the project, according to the release. Areas of inquiry are set to include studying ticks and the pathogens they carry through the lenses of genomics, the study and comparison of entire genome sequences; ecology; data science; and utilizing artificial intelligence. Studying ticks can shed light on systems larger than themselves, Needle said in the release, giving the study the potential to build understanding not only of tick-borne illnesses but of other complex, interconnected systems, too. title: UNH awarded $8M grant to study ticks - WMUR
content: Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. The University of New Hampshire is getting an $8 million grant to study ticks, the diseases they spread and the environments they thrive in. The grant from the National Science Foundation comes at a time when concern is high about tick-borne illnesses and the spread of additional tick species into the region. Recent research shows that ticks are also showing up in more cities along the East Coast, not just in wooded areas. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, New Hampshire has one of the highest rates of Lyme disease in the country. "They come in the first season, and then you're like, 'Oh they're gone.' And then October, November, you go outside, and there's ticks all over the place again," said David Needle, a clinical professor and senior veterinary pathologist who will lead the four-year initiative. "But, we're using that as like an annually renewable resource, like a repeated experiment that's there for us." The funding will focus on three tick species found in New Hampshire: the blacklegged or deer tick, the American dog tick and the winter tick, which has major impacts on moose and wildlife health. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << Researchers will investigate how ticks survive, spread and transmit disease by setting up 22 stations across the state. "From those stations, we will drag for ticks during peak season," said Needle. "The stations will monitor all year round, and so we can get deeper into the question of, like, what does snow coverage do?" Needle said that portion of the research will start at the beginning of the next peak season. Thousands of people get Lyme disease every year, and ticks are known to be a menace in New Hampshire as the disease they carry requires extra precautions. "It's been a difficult time because I live in Dunbarton, so I live in like, the woody area," said Kennith Dibattista of Dunbarton. Pets, such as dogs, also require prevention from tickborne illnesses. "You know, it was really, really bad last year, so I decided to do the heartworm plus the tick preventative monthly pill, as well as the collars that prevent ticks as well," said Chantel McMillan of Manchester. The multimillion-dollar grant also has an educational component, as undergraduate students from across the Granite State will assist with the research.
